newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo truce shaken, Africans back peace force.
newsitem.headline: Congo truce shaken, Africans back peace force.

text.p: A 90-minute artillery duel between factions supporting Congo's president and a bitter rival shook a six-day-old ceasefire in Brazzaville on Monday, as support grew for a peace force.

Eight Francophone West African states, whose leaders met in a summit in Togo, expressed support for efforts to pull together a peacekeeping force for Brazzaville. Officials from Senegal and Togo said they would contribute troops.
Supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, have been fighting each other off and on in Brazzaville since June 5.

Monday's battle was the worst breach of the truce called on June 17, and seemed close to scuppering already strained efforts by local mediator, Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, to prevent a return to all-out hostilities.
French ambassador Raymond Cesaire told Reuters Congo's parliament -- which was to have met on Monday -- seemed to have been a target during the heavy late-morning duel.
"It was a bit stormy all day, but it seems to be subsiding now. There are some forces who want to sow confusion to stop Kolelas proceeding with his mediation," he said.

Seven shells crossed the Congo river frontier to slam into the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, injuring no one but raising angry protests from Laurent Kabila's new government, which said it had been deliberately targeted.
"We could tell precisely where they were fired from," Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha said in a statement.
He said he was giving the unidentified guilty party a last warning that further such incidents would not be tolerated.
Mohamed Sahnoun, the United Nations special envoy for the former Zaire and Congo, told Reuters in Togo's capital Lome that the death toll from the fighting in Congo could be as high as 3,000.
Red Cross sources on the ground have estimated the number of deaths at at least 1,000.

Brazzaville was carved into opposing sectors and its centre into a no-man's-land by clashes that flared on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm a militia run by his predecessor, Sassou Nguesso, ahead of a presidential election on July 27 in which both were candidates. The poll has now been postponed.

Officials from the eight countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) -- Togo, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Guinea-Bissau and Senegal -- said a peacekeeping mission could be put together rapidly.
The leaders of the eight said in a statement their countries would be "available to take part in this peace force under the authority of the UN and the OAU (the Organisation of African Unity)".
The U.N. has insisted that before peacekeepers come, there must be peace and proof that both sides want a political solution.
During Monday's exchange at least two shells slammed into houses near a crowded market in Bacongo, wounding six people. Kolelas's militia, which has kept out of the fighting so far, controls Bacongo.
Frightened civilians, fearing the war was spreading, crammed into trucks and left for the countryside, untouched by fighting.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), whose teams have stopped work because of the dangers, said there were no serious problems in the paralysed city with food, water or sanitation.
